Uses a different user, only two articles, and no waits, so timestamps may tie. With ties, the reverse-sorted check passes even for wrong ordering, so the test cannot reliably detect a violation. The strict datetime format parse may also fail on a correct response.

Uses random users and 3 articles instead of the specified feedpageuser1/feedpageauthor1 accounts and 5 articles. It asserts articlesCount==3 rather than 5, and offset=2 yields 1 article, not 2. It also checks a newest-first order the requirement never states, which can be flaky on ties. It does catch ignored limit or offset, so pagination logic is partly covered.

The test follows the general follow/unfollow flow, but it uses randomly named users instead of the specified ones. Its GET profile checks after following and unfollowing are unauthenticated, though the requirement says to use user1's token. A correct implementation would likely report following=false there, so the test would fail on correct behaviour.

Covers the full follow/unfollow lifecycle and asserts the 'following' flag at each step as required. It omits the required check that username is 'profiletarget1' and uses different usernames, emails and passwords than specified. The extra unauthenticated check is only a type check, so it should not break a correct implementation.

Covers comment creation, unique integer IDs and body presence, but does not use the specified user1 credentials or article title. It never asserts exactly 3 comments are returned, only that at least 3 matching ones exist. Passes a correct implementation but could miss an extra or duplicate comment.

Follows the required follow/unfollow sequence and checks the 'following' flag at each step. It omits the required username check and uses different usernames and emails than specified. It asserts follow returns 201, which the requirement does not state and a correct implementation may not return, so it could fail on correct behaviour.

The test creates both users and articles as specified, then filters by author and asserts articlesCount is 1 and that the only returned article has the expected title, covering every stated outcome. It relies on standard RealWorld-style status codes and response shapes, which are a small risk if the implementation differs.

Sets up the stated scenario (user, article, three comments) and asserts all stated outcomes: count of 3, unique ids, and preserved bodies. Extra checks on integer ids and timestamp/author fields go beyond the requirement and could fail a correct implementation that uses other id types.

Tests two same-title articles get distinct slugs, but uses a different title and a timestamp-generated user instead of the specified user1 and 'Duplicate Title Article'. Asserts an assumed lowercase-alphanumeric suffix format not required by the spec, which could fail a correct implementation.

The test uses different users and titles than specified, never checks articlesCount or the article titles, and adds an unfollow step the requirement omits. It passes fixture function objects to json, which would raise a serialization error. The final cleanup also reads tokens from the wrong response, so it would fail even on a correct implementation.

The test logs in as a different user (test@example.com), not the required user1 'sluguser1', and uses a random title rather than 'Duplicate Title Article'. It asserts the slug equals a predicted value, including a random suffix it cannot know, so it would fail on correct implementations. It never checks that slugs differ or start with the required prefix.

Covers every step: register user, create article, verify it in the global list with the author, attempt deletion by email expecting 500, then verify the article persists. Minor risk from the unrequired 'errors' key check and the unwrapped article response shape assertions, which could fail a correct implementation.

Covers the core flow: comment creation, retrieval by GET, and an integer id. It omits the required check of the POST response's comments array. It uses a random user, a different article title and a different comment body than specified, and accepts 201 as well as 200. It also asserts extra fields such as author username and created/updated, which the requirement does not state.

Creates the user, decodes the JWT payload, and checks username, email and GET /api/user. It only checks that 'id' exists in the payload and never compares it to the created user's id, which the requirement requires. Base64 decoding uses standard b64decode, which can corrupt base64url characters, so a correct implementation could fail.

The test covers the post-follow feed: it checks articlesCount is 1, the article's author is the followed user, and the unfollowed user's article is absent. It omits the required initial check that the feed is empty (articlesCount 0) before any follow. Its checks on the followed article use author rather than the exact title. It should pass on a correct implementation and catch feeds that include unfollowed authors' articles.

The test does not follow the requirement. It uses a different user ('testuser123'), calls DELETE /api/user instead of /api/users/<email>, and expects 422 rather than 500. Covers the required articlesCount of 5, the 2-article page, and a distinct second page. It also asserts an exact title order (Article 5, 4, then 3, 2), which the requirement does not state and which could fail on a correct implementation with tied timestamps or different ordering.

The test asserts a 404 after deletion, but the requirement demands a 200 with an empty object. It also skips the pre-delete GET check, uses a different user and title, and never asserts the 200 status on the post-deletion GET. A correct implementation would fail it.

The test ignores the required users (feedpageuser1/feedpageauthor1), follow relationship, and five articles. It registers a different user and uses weak assertions like '>= 0' and '<= 20', so it would not detect the required behaviour being broken.

Covers the required checks: articlesCount of 5, two articles returned for limit=2, and a distinct second page. It adds unstated assertions, notably exact reverse-chronological slug order and a third page, which could fail a correct implementation. It also uses random users instead of the specified usernames and emails.

Covers the full flow and the stated assertions. However, it reads the POST response as an unwrapped article object but expects the GET response wrapped under 'article'. Covers the full flow: user creation, article creation, GET before and after DELETE, and the 200 status on DELETE. It also asserts the DELETE body equals {}, which the requirement does not state and could fail a correct implementation. The post-delete GET check matches the requirement.

The test creates the user and three articles with the specified titles and tags, then checks articlesCount and titles for tag=javascript, tag=testing and tag=nonexistent, covering every stated outcome. Extra assertions on creation responses (tagList echo) are reasonable. Minor risk from the fixed username or response-shape assumptions, but a correct implementation should pass.

The test is a syntactically invalid stub: 'def test_follow_status' has no colon, parameters or body. It will fail at collection on any implementation and asserts none of the required follow-status behaviour, so it neither passes correctly nor detects violations.

The test follows every step: creates the user and article, confirms the article via GET, asserts DELETE returns 500, and confirms the article still exists. Checks are exact to the requirement. The test contains only import statements and no test function, setup, requests, or assertions. It exercises none of the required create, follow, unfollow, profile-check, or self-unfollow behaviour, so it cannot verify the requirement or detect violations.

Covers all stated steps: 201 on creation, then 400 with the required message for both duplicate-username and duplicate-email cases. Overall is reduced because it assumes a specific error shape (errors.body list) and checks extra response fields (token, bio, image) the requirement does not mention, which could fail a correct implementation with a different format.

The test covers every stated step: creates both users, checks following is false, follows, checks true with the correct username, unfollows, and checks false again. Minor risks: it strictly requires 200 on follow and DELETE for unfollow, and asserts extra profile fields, which a correct implementation might vary on.

The test follows the requirement: it creates both users, has user2 publish an article, then asserts user1's feed has articlesCount 0 and an empty articles array. However, the cleanup calls DELETE /users/{username} and asserts status 200, which is not a standard RealWorld endpoint. If it returns an error, the test fails even when the feed behaviour is correct.

Covers the required delete-then-GET-404 flow and asserts 200 on delete. It uses a different title than specified and adds unstated checks: 201 on create, exact field names accessToken/tokenType, and a list check. These could fail a correct implementation.

Covers the required register-then-login flow: checks register returns 200 and login returns an accessToken. The test registers and logs in both users, creates one todo each, and asserts userA's GET returns exactly one todo titled 'UserA Todo', covering the isolation requirement. Some unstated details (exact status codes, the accessToken field name, the isComplete type) could fail a correct implementation that differs in those conventions.

Sets up both users, creates userA's todo, and asserts userB gets 404, matching the requirement. However, it also asserts an empty 404 body and an integer ID type, which the requirement does not state. A correct implementation returning an error JSON body would fail the test.

Covers every stated step: two registrations, logins, owner creates todo, other user's PUT expects 404, owner GET confirms title unchanged. Minor risks: assumes 200 for registration and an 'accessToken' field name, which a correct implementation could differ on.

Covers every required step: register, login, create, DELETE expecting 200, then GET expecting 404. It also hard-codes unstated details (register returns 200, create returns 201, the 'accessToken' field name), which could fail a correct implementation that differs in these conventions.

The test covers the required flow: create, PUT with isComplete=true and new title, expects 200, then GET verifies both updated fields. The test follows the requirement's steps: register, login, create a todo, then PUT with a mismatched id and asserts 400. Main risk is the hardcoded 201 expectation for todo creation, which could fail a correct implementation returning 200.

Sets up register and login, then checks the 400 status and the errors structure for a title key. Sets up two users, creates a todo as user1, and asserts that user2's GET returns 404, which is the required outcome.
